table.caption: Who decides in three invented countries (invented data for practice)
cols: Who owns most factories and farms
rows: firms, guided by what buyers pay
mostly private owners; the state runs the railways
mostly firms; the government provides schools and roads

economic-systems-s2.title: Tessaly's winter coats
economic-systems-s2.text: In the invented country of Tessaly, a central planning office decides how many coats the state-owned clothing factories make each year and sets the price of every coat. This year the office ordered 2 million summer jackets and 1 million winter coats. By December, stores have racks of unsold summer jackets, while winter coats are gone within days of each delivery and long lines form whenever a truck arrives. The price of a winter coat stays where the office set it.

items.q: Which three questions must every economic system answer?
options: Who votes, who governs, and who pays the taxes
How much to save, borrow and lend
What to produce, how to produce it, and for whom
Which goods to import, export and tax

why.correct: Scarcity means every society must decide what to make, how to make it and who gets it. Systems differ in who answers.
options: Those are questions about government, not how resources are allocated.
Saving and borrowing are choices inside a system, not its three questions.
Right: what, how and for whom.
Trade and taxes are policies, not the three basic questions.

items.q: In a market economy, what mainly coordinates the choices of millions of buyers and sellers?
options: Prices
A central planning board
Tradition passed down in families
Votes held for each good

why.correct: Prices carry information about what buyers want and what it costs to make, and they give people reasons to act on it.
options: Right: prices coordinate.
A planning board coordinates a command economy.
Tradition decided production in some older societies, not in a market economy.
Markets do not vote on each good.

items.q: Which kind of economic system does Brennick have?
options: A market economy
A mixed economy that relies mostly on markets
A system with no answer to "what to produce"
A command economy

why.correct: In Brennick the state owns the factories and farms and a planning board sets prices and decides what is made: a command economy.
options: In a market economy private owners and prices decide; Brennick uses a board.
Brennick's board makes the main decisions, not markets.
Every system answers it; in Brennick the board does.
Right: central ownership and a central plan.

items.q: Which kind of economic system does Coralia have?
options: A command economy
A mixed economy
A pure market economy with no government role
A traditional economy

why.correct: Coralia relies mostly on private owners and markets, but its government runs the railways, sets some rules and provides schools and roads: a mixed economy.
options: Most decisions in Coralia are made by firms and markets, not a central plan.
Right: markets plus a government role.
The government runs railways and provides schools and roads, so markets are not acting alone.
Nothing in the table says decisions follow custom.

items.q: In which country does a change in what buyers are willing to pay most directly change what gets made?
options: Brennick
Arvel
Coralia's railways
Coralia, for its schools and roads

why.correct: In Arvel firms decide what to make guided by what buyers pay, so a change in prices changes production directly.
options: Brennick's planning board decides, whatever buyers would pay.
Right: firms follow what buyers pay.
Coralia's railways are run by the state, not guided by prices.
Coralia's government provides its schools and roads, whatever buyers would pay.

items.q: In Arvel, who answers "for whom" goods are produced?
options: The national planning board
Whoever lines up first
The government, by handing out goods equally
Buyers willing and able to pay

why.correct: In a market economy, goods go to the people who are willing and able to pay for them, which depends on their incomes and wants.
options: Arvel has no planning board; that is Brennick.
Prices, not lines, ration goods in a market.
Equal hand-outs are a choice a government might make, not how Arvel works.
Right: willingness and ability to pay.

items.q: What kind of economic system does the scenario describe for Tessaly's clothing?
options: A command economy
A market economy
A mixed economy run by markets
An economy without scarcity

why.correct: A central office decides how much is made and sets prices in state-owned factories: a command system.
options: Right: central planning and state ownership.
In a market, prices and private firms would decide.
The planning office, not markets, decides here.
Coats run out within days, so scarcity is clearly present.

items.q: Why do winter coats run out while summer jackets pile up?
options: Tessaly has no factories able to sew coats
Buyers in Tessaly have no money
The fixed price sends no signal to make more coats
Coats are a factor of production

why.correct: With prices set by the office, nothing rises to tell factories that coats are wanted, and no one gains by switching from jackets to coats.
options: The factories already make 1 million coats, so they can sew them.
Long lines show people are trying to buy.
Right: a fixed price sends no signal.
Coats are a finished good, not a resource used in production.

items.q: If coat prices were set in a market instead, what would most likely happen?
options: Coat prices would fall, and firms would make fewer coats
Nothing would change, because prices do not affect firms
Firms would make more summer jackets
Coat prices would rise, so firms make more coats

why.correct: Buyers lining up for coats would push the price up. A higher price makes coats more rewarding to produce, so firms shift resources toward coats.
options: Strong buying pushes a market price up, not down.
Prices change what firms can earn, so they change what firms make.
Jackets are piling up, so a market would send resources away from them.
Right: higher price, more coats.

items.q: Who answers "what to produce" for Tessaly's clothing?
options: The buyers in the lines
The store clerks
The central planning office
The workers in each factory, by vote

why.correct: The office orders 2 million jackets and 1 million coats, so it decides what is made.
options: Buyers line up, but their wants do not change the plan.
Clerks sell what arrives; they do not decide what is made.
Right: the office sets the output.
Nothing in the scenario says workers vote on output.
Rules that set the price of each good
Legal rights to own, use and gain from property
Government ownership of factories
Rights to receive goods for free

why.correct: Property rights say who owns something and let the owner use it, sell it and keep what it earns.
options: Price setting is a different policy.
Right: ownership and its rewards.
That describes state ownership, the opposite of private property.
Owning something is not a right to free goods.

items.q: Why do well-defined property rights help a market economy work?
options: Owners keep what they earn, so they have reason to produce
They let the government set the prices of goods
They promise each firm that it will make a profit
They remove scarcity

why.correct: If you can keep the rewards of building or improving something, you have a reason to do it. Without secure ownership, that reason weakens.
options: Right: secure rewards create incentives.
Property rights let owners, not the government, decide.
Owners can still lose money; rights do not promise a profit.
Scarcity remains in every system.

items.q: A country lets private firms make most goods, but its government runs public schools, builds highways and sets safety rules. Which system is this?
options: A pure market economy
A command economy
A mixed economy
An economy with no government

why.correct: Markets plus a government that provides some goods and makes rules is a mixed economy.
options: A pure market economy would leave schools and highways to private firms too.
Most goods here come from private firms, not a central plan.
Right: markets with a government role.
The government plays a clear role here.

items.q: A sneaker company sees its new model selling out and its price rising on resale sites. It moves workers from older models to the new one. Which idea does this show?
options: Prices steer resources toward what buyers want
A central plan tells the firm what to make
The firm ignores prices when choosing what to make
Workers in a firm stay on the products they started on

why.correct: The higher price shows buyers value the new model, and making more of it is more rewarding, so the firm moves labor toward it.
options: Right: prices guide where resources go.
No planner is involved; the firm reacts to prices.
The firm reacts directly to the price signal.
The firm just moved workers from one model to another.

items.q: Which statement compares market and command economies accurately?
options: Market economies face scarcity and command economies do not
Command economies get by without any prices
Market economies get by without any government
Markets coordinate by prices; command economies by plans

why.correct: Both face scarcity and both have prices and governments; the difference is who decides and what coordinates the decisions.
options: Scarcity is universal.
Command economies set prices by plan rather than letting markets set them.
Every real market economy has a government that enforces contracts and property rights.
Right: prices versus plans.

items.q: Which of these are institutions a market economy relies on? Select all that apply.
options: Enforceable contracts
Property rights
A planning board that sets output
Prices fixed by the government for each good

why.correct: Markets need rules that let people own things and trust deals: property rights, contracts and the rule of law.
options: Right: deals must be enforceable.
Right: owners must be able to keep and use what they own.
Setting output by plan is how a command economy works.
Market prices come from buyers and sellers, not government decree.

items.q: In a market economy, buyers suddenly want more electric bikes. Put the steps in order.
options: Buyers want more electric bikes than stores have
The price of electric bikes rises
Making electric bikes becomes more rewarding for firms
Firms move resources into making more electric bikes

why.correct: Wants change, the price signals it, the higher price creates an incentive, and firms respond by shifting resources.
